concepts.title: The Native Peoples of the Americas and Australia
concepts.definition: Before the Europeans, the Americas were home to native peoples from the Inuit of the Arctic to the Aztecs and Incas with organised empires, and Australia was held by Aboriginal communities for tens of thousands of years, each with distinct cultures tied to their lands.
concepts.key_idea: The native peoples lived by hunting, gathering and agriculture, and their societies were altered forever by European colonisation after 1492.

concepts.title: European Colonisation and Displacement of the Natives
concepts.definition: European settlers displaced indigenous peoples through war, disease like smallpox, land hunger and broken treaties, pushing natives onto reservations, as in the westward expansion of the United States and the settler colonisation of Australia under the doctrine that the land belonged to no one.
concepts.key_idea: Gold, plantations and railroads drove natives from their lands, and by the late nineteenth century the native population had fallen drastically with their cultures under attack.

concepts.title: Later Reassessment: Native Voices and Cultural Survival
concepts.definition: In the twentieth century indigenous peoples reasserted their identities through cultural revival, land claims and museums telling their own histories, and countries began recognising native rights and the injustices of settler history.
concepts.key_idea: History written from native perspectives recasts the pioneers of settler lore as invaders, and demands for native languages, land and dignity continue today.
